selection_principle: Prefer traceable real Spark/YARN incidents and questions. Community/JIRA cases establish ecological relevance only; correctness comes from frozen Spark 3.5.9 constraints and execution.

sources.title: Conflicting spark-defaults.conf and spark-submit values: which wins?
sources.real_problem: A user asks whether a value in spark-defaults.conf or a different value passed to spark-submit has priority.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 documents SparkConf > spark-submit flags > spark-defaults.conf precedence.
potential_task_forms: conflicting executor-memory values across defaults and CLI
conflicting executor-cores values across defaults and CLI
sources.notes: Strong provenance case; exact answer must be re-derived from Spark 3.5.9 docs, not copied from the old answer.

sources.title: What is the priority among SparkConf, spark-submit, spark-env.sh and spark-defaults.conf?
sources.real_problem: A user is confused about configuration precedence and the role of spark-env.sh versus Spark properties.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 distinguishes Spark properties from environment variables and documents property precedence.
potential_task_forms: choose the correct source for a Spark property
distinguish Spark property from per-machine environment configuration
sources.notes: May be useful for source-selection tasks, but avoid broad spark-env.sh questions that are not automatically assertable. Re-screened after frozen precedence/source validation; suitable as provenance only.

sources.title: Load Spark settings from multiple configuration files
sources.real_problem: A user wants Spark to load spark-defaults.conf plus another properties file with last-file-wins behavior.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 supports spark-defaults.conf and --properties-file behavior through spark-submit, but arbitrary multi-file merge semantics are not a general built-in precedence layer.
potential_task_forms: select one properties file with --properties-file
reason about whether two property files are automatically merged
sources.notes: Do not admit until properties-file fixture/runner behavior is validated. R09_PROPERTIES_FILE PASS on Spark 3.5.9; later --load-spark-defaults case dropped.

sources.title: spark-submit with --properties-file still reports missing application resource
sources.real_problem: A user puts Spark properties in a file but omits the actual application resource and gets Missing application resource.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: spark-submit syntax still requires an application resource; the benchmark runner intentionally supplies fixed ConfigProbe itself.
sources.notes: Valuable real case, but Formal Benchmark should not let the model supply the application jar/class. Keep as design rationale for fixed ConfigProbe.

sources.title: How to set spark.driver.memory in client mode
sources.real_problem: A user asks why setting driver memory after Spark has already initialized is ineffective and where it should be set.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 explicitly says client-mode driver memory must not be set through SparkConf after the driver JVM has started; use --driver-memory or default properties.
potential_task_forms: client mode driver memory via --driver-memory
reject application SparkConf as the sole source for client-mode driver memory
sources.notes: High-value placement task. Needs a client-mode fixture/probe before whitelist admission. R07A/R07B runtime validation PASS.

sources.title: Driver configured with 10g but actually runs with 1g in client mode
sources.real_problem: A real OOM case traced to setting spark.driver.memory in Spark configuration while running in client mode.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Same Spark 3.5.9 client-mode driver-memory placement rule as RC005.
potential_task_forms: repair an ineffective client-mode driver-memory placement
sources.notes: Excellent real incident for repair-style wording later; first validate placement behavior in the harness. R07A/R07B runtime validation PASS.

sources.title: Trying to switch to YARN cluster deploy mode from SparkSession code
sources.real_problem: A user tries to set master/deploy mode inside application code and receives an error indicating cluster deploy mode is not applicable to the shell.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark submission docs define --master yarn and --deploy-mode cluster as submission-time deployment choices.
potential_task_forms: generate YARN cluster-mode submission settings
distinguish master from deploy mode
sources.notes: Use only the deployment semantics, not PySpark-shell-specific details.

sources.title: Submitting to remote YARN and choosing the correct master
sources.real_problem: A user confuses HDFS URLs with the Spark/YARN master and asks how a remote client selects YARN.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: For this benchmark, master is fixed to yarn; cluster endpoints are inherited from Hadoop/YARN configuration.
sources.notes: Real but infrastructure-heavy; avoid making cluster endpoint/HADOOP_CONF_DIR management part of first-paper benchmark.

sources.title: spark-submit options placed after application resource are interpreted as application arguments
sources.real_problem: A user places --deploy-mode and --master after the application jar and does not get the intended submission behavior.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: spark-submit syntax places Spark options before the application resource; the study's safe builder supplies the fixed resource.
sources.notes: Useful justification for never executing raw model command text; safe builder canonicalizes argv and supplies ConfigProbe resource.

sources.title: Legacy yarn-cluster versus --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster
sources.real_problem: A real question discusses yarn-cluster and the equivalent modern separation of master and deploy mode.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 submission uses master=yarn and deploy-mode=cluster; the current harness already rejects literal yarn-cluster.
potential_task_forms: convert a legacy yarn-cluster intent into Spark 3.5.9 master/deploy-mode settings
detect invalid legacy master value
sources.notes: Already covered as a blocked C3 case; good negative task provenance.

sources.title: Submitting a Spark job to a specific YARN queue
sources.real_problem: A user wants a Spark application to run in a particular YARN queue rather than the default queue.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 documents spark.yarn.queue / --queue as the YARN queue for submission.
potential_task_forms: submit to default queue explicitly
sources.notes: Non-default queue variants require adding and freezing a second known YARN queue before Formal use.

sources.title: How to make spark-submit exit after YARN submission
sources.real_problem: Users want the submit client to return after successful YARN submission rather than wait for application completion; the research user encountered this exact behavior.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 documents spark.yarn.submit.waitAppCompletion for YARN cluster mode.
potential_task_forms: asynchronous submit client return
contrast true versus false behavior
sources.notes: One of the strongest real-world runtime-semantic cases in the current benchmark.

sources.title: What is the impact of spark.yarn.submit.waitAppCompletion=false?
sources.real_problem: A user asks what operational behavior changes when waitAppCompletion is false.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Same Spark 3.5.9 waitAppCompletion rule as RC012.
potential_task_forms: require caller to return immediately after submission while application continues
sources.notes: Use Apache Spark/YARN behavior only; do not import EMR-specific lifecycle semantics into the benchmark.

sources.title: Executor memory configured as 6G but Spark UI shows smaller storage memory
sources.real_problem: A user confuses executor heap configuration with a smaller storage-memory figure shown in the UI.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 defines spark.executor.memory as executor JVM heap; Effective SparkConf is the correct primary observation for the configured value.
potential_task_forms: set executor heap memory to a requested value
distinguish configured heap from derived UI storage-memory metrics
sources.notes: Formal task should ask for executor heap, not ask model to calculate storage memory.

sources.title: YARN container killed for exceeding memory limits; memoryOverhead confusion
sources.real_problem: A YARN application is killed for exceeding container memory and the user asks how executor heap and overhead relate.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 uses spark.executor.memoryOverhead; executor container memory includes heap plus overhead and other documented components.
potential_task_forms: set executor memory overhead explicitly
combine executor heap and overhead constraints
sources.notes: Very valuable real incident; add spark.executor.memoryOverhead to rule catalog and validate YARN resource observation before use. R08 runtime allocation revalidation PASS.

sources.title: Is spark.yarn.executor.memoryOverhead deprecated / renamed?
sources.real_problem: A user notices an older YARN-specific memory-overhead key disappearing from docs and asks what property to use.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 current property is spark.executor.memoryOverhead.
potential_task_forms: use the current Spark 3.5.9 memory-overhead key rather than legacy YARN-specific naming
sources.notes: Good version-drift task if the legacy alias behavior is explicitly tested before Formal inclusion. R08 validated current spark.executor.memoryOverhead behavior.

sources.title: Difference between --num-executors and --executor-cores on YARN
sources.real_problem: A user asks whether executor count and cores per executor represent the same resource dimension.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark submission exposes distinct executor-instances and executor-cores settings.
potential_task_forms: request N executors with C cores each
multi-constraint executor count + cores + memory
sources.notes: Strong basis for composition tasks; A3/C3 already exercised executor cores and instances.

sources.title: Is --num-executors per node or total across the YARN application?
sources.real_problem: A user is unsure whether --num-executors is a per-node quantity or the application's executor count.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: spark.executor.instances / --num-executors controls the application executor count under static allocation.
potential_task_forms: request an exact total executor count
combine instances and cores without interpreting instances as per-node
sources.notes: Useful intent-mapping task.

sources.title: Can --num-executors override dynamic allocation?
sources.real_problem: A user asks how static executor instances interact with dynamic allocation and initial executor count.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 documents that if spark.executor.instances is larger than dynamicAllocation.initialExecutors, the initial executor count uses the larger value.
potential_task_forms: set dynamic allocation bounds and an initial executor count
reason about executor.instances interaction with initialExecutors
sources.notes: Do not Formal-freeze until dynamic allocation runtime probe can observe initial/scale behavior robustly. R11 initial-executor precedence runtime validation PASS.

sources.title: Relationship among maxExecutors, num-executors and initialExecutors
sources.real_problem: A user observes apparently conflicting dynamic-allocation settings and asks which determines the initial executor count.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 current configuration rules must be used; community answers span older Spark versions.
potential_task_forms: initial/min/max executor composition
sources.notes: Excellent version-drift example; source provides problem provenance, not oracle. R11 initial-executor precedence runtime validation PASS.

sources.title: Does dynamic allocation require external shuffle service?
sources.real_problem: A recent user asks whether dynamic allocation still depends on an external shuffle service; Spark itself added shuffle tracking and later enabled it by default.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Spark 3.5.9 supports dynamic allocation with shuffle tracking; shuffleTracking.enabled defaults to true.
potential_task_forms: enable dynamic allocation on a cluster without external shuffle service using supported Spark 3.5.9 behavior
sources.notes: Very strong real-world dependency task; current A3 proved acceptance/executor launch but not full scale-up/scale-down behavior. R10 scale-up/scale-down runtime validation PASS; R06 upgraded to whitelist YES.

sources.title: Prevent --conf in spark-submit from overriding spark-defaults.conf
sources.real_problem: A deployment owner wants baseline settings in spark-defaults.conf to remain effective even when users pass conflicting --conf values, directly exposing Spark configuration precedence as an operational concern.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Use only the problem as provenance; correctness is re-derived from frozen Spark 3.5.9 precedence behavior.
potential_task_forms: override a conflicting default for one submission
keep non-conflicting defaults while overriding one property
sources.notes: Recent real case. Community answer is not the oracle.

sources.title: Set Spark configuration and understand precedence
sources.real_problem: A user asks where to set Spark properties and how values from SparkConf, spark-submit and spark-defaults.conf interact.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Use frozen Spark 3.5.9 configuration precedence and the benchmark's isolated SPARK_CONF_DIR.
potential_task_forms: place stable values in defaults
override one default via CLI while retaining another
sources.notes: Useful independent provenance beyond RC001/RC002.

sources.title: Conflict between setMaster in SparkConf and --master in spark-submit
sources.real_problem: A user supplies the master both in application SparkConf and spark-submit and asks which one wins.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Only precedence/source-placement concepts are used; benchmark remains YARN-only.
potential_task_forms: avoid conflicting master sources
express YARN master through the submission artifact
sources.notes: Source mentions standalone in the original question; Formal tasks adapt only the generic precedence issue to YARN.

sources.title: How to set driver memory in spark-submit client mode
sources.real_problem: A user running Spark in client mode asks how to set driver memory and cites the rule that driver heap must be established before the driver JVM starts.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Frozen R07 runtime probe verifies actual client driver heap.
potential_task_forms: client-mode driver heap via --driver-memory
combine driver and executor resource requests
sources.notes: Do not extend first-paper whitelist to driver memoryOverhead merely because the source mentions it.

sources.title: Spark on YARN: client vs cluster driver-memory differences
sources.real_problem: A user compares driver memory behavior under YARN client and cluster deployment.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Formal tasks use only validated driver-memory and deploy-mode semantics.
potential_task_forms: client-mode driver placement
cluster versus client deployment composition
sources.notes: UI memory fractions from the source are not imported into the oracle.

sources.title: Apache Spark differences between client and cluster deploy modes
sources.real_problem: A user asks where the driver runs and what operational difference client versus cluster deploy mode makes.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Use frozen YARN deployment semantics only.
potential_task_forms: keep driver on submit host with client mode
place driver under YARN with cluster mode
sources.notes: Generic deploy-mode provenance.

sources.title: How to choose the queue for a Spark job using spark-submit
sources.real_problem: A user asks how to submit a Spark application to a chosen YARN queue.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: P0 exposes only the default queue; Formal variants therefore use queue=default unless the cluster profile is changed and re-frozen.
potential_task_forms: explicitly select the default queue
combine queue selection with client or cluster mode
sources.notes: Independent real queue provenance.

sources.title: How to check if a Spark streaming job is running
sources.real_problem: A user wants the local submit process to remain alive so its lifetime can be used when monitoring a YARN cluster application.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Use only the validated waitAppCompletion=true/false behavior in YARN cluster mode.
potential_task_forms: keep submit client alive until completion
contrast monitored versus asynchronous submission
sources.notes: Complements RC012/RC013 with the wait=true use case.

sources.title: How to specify the number of executors to hold an RDD
sources.real_problem: A user asks how executor count is specified and the spark-submit help text also shows the relationship with dynamic allocation initial executors.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Formal tasks use only frozen R12/R13/R11 behavior, not workload-sizing advice.
potential_task_forms: exact total executor count
combine executor count and cores
dynamic initial-count composition
sources.notes: Useful real resource-intent provenance.

sources.title: Should executor cores be set to one in YARN mode?
sources.real_problem: A user asks whether one executor core means a single-threaded executor and discusses resource shaping.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Formal tasks ask only for exact per-executor core counts, not tuning recommendations.
potential_task_forms: request two or three cores per executor
combine cores with a fixed executor count
sources.notes: No performance-optimality claims are imported.

sources.title: How to set executor number by memory in YARN mode
sources.real_problem: A user asks how executor counts are bounded by YARN resources and how dynamic allocation min/max affect executor numbers.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Use frozen executor-count and dynamic-allocation semantics; do not turn the task into performance sizing.
potential_task_forms: bounded dynamic executor count
static total executor count under YARN
sources.notes: Resource-sizing advice from answers is not an oracle.

sources.title: Why increase spark.yarn.executor.memoryOverhead?
sources.real_problem: A user sees YARN kill an executor container for exceeding physical memory and asks what memory overhead represents.
sources.spark_3_5_9_basis: Formal tasks use current Spark 3.5.9 spark.executor.memoryOverhead and frozen YARN allocation observations.

reason about container allocation versus heap

sources.title: Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits on EMR

sources.title: Spark job failed with container killed by YARN for exceeding physical memory limits
sources.real_problem: A 2024 Spark job uses explicit executor heap and memory overhead but still encounters YARN physical-memory kills.

compose heap and overhead with other resource constraints
sources.notes: Recent incident provenance; not a tuning oracle.

sources.title: Check if External Shuffle Service is enabled on a YARN cluster
